text.p: The following is a direct contribution from commodity statistician F.O. Licht in Ratzeburg, Germany. Please address any queries to Helmut Ahlfeld on +00 49 4541 88920.

White sugar futures in London ended higher in quiet trade. Gains in New York underpinned the London market. May ended $3.10 higher at $307.60 per tonne, while August added $2.0 to close at $305.60 per tonne. Raw sugar futures in New York ended higher across the board on late session speculative short-covering. May ended up 14 points to close at 10.90 cents/lb, while July added 11 points to close at 10.63 cents/lb. The outer months gained between 7 and 11 points. Analysts said near-term resistance in May can be found at 11.00 cents/lb and then at the recent high of 11.09 cents/lb. However, prices are expected to remain within their current trading range amid a dearth of fundamental news. China reiterated that it would not be importing sugar in 1997 but this was nothing new and can be doubted.

CHINA - China is unlikely to import sugar in 1997 because of sufficient domestic supply as well as imports already agreed from Cuba and recent high levels of smuggling, Chinese press reports said. It was added that sugar production in 1996/97 (September/August) can be estimated at 6.6 mn tonnes, white value, while consumption was put at 7.5 mn tonnes. It was said that imports of Cuban sugar through bilateral agreements, coupled with domestic reserves and the entry of large amounts of smuggled sugar from 1995 to early 1996 would fill the gap. However, China does not only import sugar for domestic consumption but also for tolling depending on the whites premium. Some sugar was already imported from Australia and Hong Kong this year.

THAILAND - There seems to be some confusion about the crop progress in Thailand. According to ISO figures, sugar production in January 1997 amounted to 1.995 million tonnes, raw value, up from last year's 1.709 million tonnes. This brought cumulative production in November/January up to 2.593 million tonnes compared to 2.475 million tonnes in the like period the previous year. According to figures supplied by the Ministry of Industry the current crop continued to trail behind the previous year's results throughout January and February and only at the beginning of March output was higher than in 1995/96. Total Thai sugar production in 1996/97 is estimated at around 6.5 million tonnes, slightly up on last year's 6.3 million tonnes.

CZECH REPUBLIC - Sugar exports in January 1997 amounted to 6,243 tonnes, raw value, up on last year's 1,892 tonnes. This brought cumulative production in the first five months of 1996/97 up to 26,783 tonnes, more than twice as much as last year's 13,059 tonnes. The Czech sugar surplus is estimated at 100,000 to 150,000 tonnes, white value, after a bumper crop of 610,000 tonnes, white value in 1996/97. However, due to high internal production costs it remains to be seen whether the country will be able to ship its complete surplus.

IRELAND - Sugar exports in October 1996, the first month of the 1996/97 campaign, reached 4,867 tonnes, raw value, slightly up on last year's 4,602 tonnes. Total exports in 1995/96 amounted to 74,907 tonnes compared to 56,773 tonnes in 1994/95. Ireland exports most of its sugar to neighbouring United Kingdom with additional tonnages going to Israel and Turkey in 1995/96.
